messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 42
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Tax Inspector
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident, Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events, Event Recall: Talking about the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened, Downward Comparison: I remind myself it could have been worse, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
  Negative Appraisals: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Vignette:
Rohan, a forty-two-year-old tax inspector, found his life irrevocably altered one rainy Tuesday afternoon a year and a half ago. He had been driving home, tired after a long day of auditing, when a moment of distraction led to his car hydroplaning. He remembered the sickening screech of tires, the metallic groan as his vehicle slammed into the rear of another sedan, and the subsequent chain reaction involving a third car. What haunted him most was the sight of the crumpled passenger side of the car he hit, and the agonizing screams that followed. He later learned the driver had sustained severe, life-altering injuries.

In the immediate aftermath, Rohan’s memory of the event was a jumble of fragmented sensory input. He often found himself replaying the crash in his mind, and when he did, he sometimes heard the distinct, horrifying sound of shattering glass and the injured driver’s cries as clearly as if they were happening in the room with him. Yet, despite these vivid auditory flashes, he felt like he was only remembering parts of what happened; the full picture remained frustratingly out of reach, like a puzzle with crucial pieces missing. Some moments, like the sight of the mangled steel, were extremely clear, almost painfully so, while others, particularly the moments leading up to the impact, were completely blank.

Since the accident, Rohan had come to believe that his world had been completely destroyed. He had always seen himself as a careful, responsible man, a pillar of his community, but the accident shattered those beliefs entirely. He felt a deep, pervasive sense of humiliation, convinced that he was permanently marked by his failure. What frightened him most was the crushing weight of responsibility; he was certain he should have protected the other driver, and he felt he had profoundly failed them. This internal narrative of failure and shame became a constant companion.

His days were now punctuated by sudden jolts of fear. Driving to his office, a modern glass-fronted building in the city center, became an ordeal. The sight of cars hit by accident, even minor fender-benders on the news, sent a jolt of anxiety through him, triggering vivid, unwanted images of his own crash. He found himself taking longer, circuitous routes to work, trying to avoid busy intersections where he might witness such scenes. Funerals, cemeteries, or any grief-related events, even a distant obituary in the newspaper, would plunge him into a profound despair, reminding him of the precariousness of life and the suffering he had caused. He also went to great lengths to suppress thoughts about the trauma, actively pushing away any intrusive memories or images, which only seemed to make them stronger. He would quickly change the TV channel if a car accident was reported, or abruptly end conversations if they veered towards discussions of loss or tragedy.

This avoidance extended to personal conversations. His wife, Priya, had tried to talk to him about the accident, sensing his distress, but Rohan would shut down, making it clear he didn't want to revisit the event. He saw talking about the event as a dangerous trigger, one that would only exacerbate his internal turmoil. He had also developed a rigid internal dialogue, telling himself he deserved to suffer because of what happened, a form of punishment thinking that dictated many of his choices. He would often deny himself small pleasures, refusing to buy new clothes or go out with friends, convinced he didn't warrant happiness. Occasionally, he would try to find some relief by reminding himself it could have been worse, that at least no one had died, but this downward comparison offered little solace and quickly evaporated under the weight of his guilt.

Over the past year, these patterns had solidified into habits. His long hours at work, once a sign of dedication, became a form of self-flagellation, a way to occupy his mind and punish himself. He’d stay late, meticulously poring over tax returns, the precise, ordered nature of the work a stark contrast to the chaos in his mind. This dedication, however, had come at a cost to his marriage; Priya felt increasingly isolated, sensing a growing distance and a wall of silence between them. Rohan's emotional withdrawal and his constant state of internal turmoil had eroded their intimacy, leaving him feeling more alone than ever.

The cumulative toll of his suffering finally pushed Rohan to seek help. He had woken up one morning feeling utterly exhausted, the weight of his unaddressed guilt and the relentless suppression of his thoughts having become unbearable. He knew he couldn't continue living this way, constantly bracing himself against the next trigger, trapped in a cycle of self-punishment and fear. He came to therapy hoping for some reprieve, but also deeply afraid that confronting the memories would only confirm his darkest fears about himself.
